To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

high expressed emotion (a risk factor for relapse of schizophrenia) in carers of people with a first episode of schizophrenia was predicted by their appraisal of the situation (their subjective burden, their avoidant coping and their perception of their relative's interpersonal functioning) and not by the illness characteristics of the relative.

even at the first episode high expressed emotion ( EE) characterises over 50% of carer–patient relationships, and that high EE is associated with high carer distress and high carer subjective burden, and low carer perception of the patient's interpersonal functioning.
carers’ appraisal of their situation is influential in determining their expressed emotion at the first episode.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and evaluation of interventions for the treatment of schizophrenia, and in particular, the development of psychological interventions to help patients with schizophrenia to improve their social and occupational functioning.
the development and evaluation of a model of expressed emotion (EE).
the role of expressed emotion in psychosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the study found high EE in carers of people with first-episode psychosis was associated with carers' appraisal of the situation and not the patient's illness.
high EE in carers of people with first-episode psychosis is associated with higher avoident coping, higher subjective burdend and lower perceived patient inter-personal functioning.
the carer’s appraisal of the patient’s behaviour is more important than the patient’s illness factors in determining high EE at the time of the first-episode of psychosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
carer appraisal is the most influential factor in determining high EE, and that it is possible to reduce or prevent high EE at the first psychotic episode.
the carer appraisal model, not illness factors, is the primary determinant of high EE in early psychosis.
high expressed emotion (or high emotional over-involvement) in carers of people with psychosis is not primarily caused by the severity of the patient’s illness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
carer appraisals are more influential than illness factors in the genesis of high EE at the first-episode psychosis.

even when a person with a mental illness is first diagnosed, the way that a family member perceives the situation is a key predictor of whether that person will be a high expressed emotion carer, and this perception is influenced by how the person with the illness is coping and by how much the carer feels burdened by the illness.
the appraisal model of expressed emotion is a useful way to think about the relationship between carers and their family member with a mental health problem.
